question: Does representing architectures, optimizers, and training as interacting associative memories at different update frequencies yield a substantively new learning paradigm and, through Delta Gradient Descent, Continuum Memory Systems, self-modifying Titans, Hope, and M3, demonstrably improve continual learning, long-context recall, language modeling, and optimization?

key_findings.claim: Nested Learning is primarily a representational framework: it models a learner as nested, multi-level, or parallel optimization problems ordered by context flow and update frequency.
key_findings.evidence: Definitions 2-4 treat components as associative memories with their own objectives and define nesting through dependency between context flows. Backpropagation, pretraining, in-context learning, meta-learning, recurrent updates, and optimizers are then placed at different levels or frequencies. The framework is broad enough to redescribe many existing systems, but the paper does not give a theorem showing that the redescription alone increases capacity or prevents forgetting.

key_findings.claim: The optimizer-as-memory view is an exact or constructed reparameterization only under the stated local objectives; it is not independent evidence that an optimizer has learned a semantic memory.
key_findings.evidence: Gradient descent is written as a proximal minimizer that maps a layer input to a local output-gradient target, and momentum is treated as a second associative memory over gradients. Appendix B constructs objectives whose minimizers reproduce AdaGrad- and Adam-like preconditioners. For Adam, the value/target and approximations are chosen post hoc from gradient statistics, so 'optimal associative memory' means optimal for that constructed elementwise L2 objective, not optimal among optimizers or for downstream learning.

anchors.section: Section 4.1 / momentum as a nested memory
Appendix B / Adam objective and approximations

key_findings.claim: The printed derivation of Delta Gradient Descent does not follow its own objective: both the target sign and the proximal learning-rate coefficient change between equations (113) and (114).
key_findings.evidence: Equation (113) defines u_t=-gradient_y L and minimizes (1/2)||W x_t-u_t||^2 + (1/(2 eta_t))||W-W_t||^2. Stationarity therefore contains (W x_t+gradient_y L)x_t^T +(1/eta_t)(W-W_t)=0. Equation (114) instead prints (W x_t-gradient_y L)x_t^T +eta_t(W-W_t)=0. Equations (115)-(121) propagate that different sign and eta convention, and equation (119)'s underbraced simplification also renders x_t^T x_t=lambda^2 inconsistently. Consequently the displayed DGD update is not derived from the displayed objective without redefining the target and reciprocal step size.

key_findings.claim: Continuum Memory System (CMS) proposes a chain of redundant memory blocks updated at different chunk frequencies, with knowledge flowing across levels through backpropagation.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines sequential, nested, and independent multi-frequency arrangements and argues that fast levels adapt quickly while slow levels retain persistent information; a forgotten item can in principle be recovered through the inter-level loop. This is an architectural proposal and intuition rather than a formal no-forgetting result, and adding levels changes parameter count, state, update schedule, and compute.

anchors.section: Section 7 / sequential, nested, and independent CMS

key_findings.claim: Self-modifying Titans makes the memory's projections, data-dependent learning rate, and forgetting factors themselves in-context-updated MLP memories; Hope composes this module with CMS.
key_findings.evidence: Rather than only updating a Titans memory matrix, the construction replaces its key, value, query, eta, and alpha mappings with associative memories that generate their own values and update chunkwise. Hope places the self-modifying module before the multi-timescale CMS; Hope-Attention replaces it with softmax attention. No convergence, stability, or continual-learning theorem is proved for these coupled self-referential updates.

key_findings.claim: Hope improves several long-context multi-association cells, but the paper's statement that it is best across all NIAH tasks and difficulties is false even among its attention-free comparison set.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports Titans above Hope on S-NIAH-2 at 4K (99.6 versus 99.2) and S-NIAH-3 at 4K (74.2 versus 73.2). Hope becomes strongest at many longer multi-key/query/value cells, for example 16K MK-NIAH 14.8 versus 9.6 for the next reported model and MQ-NIAH 14.2 versus 9.4. Softmax Transformer and Hope-Attention also dominate many single-needle cells. Thus the table supports selective long-context gains, not universal dominance.

key_findings.claim: The strongest language-modeling results are positive but combine multiple architectural changes and large training budgets, so they do not isolate the NL paradigm, CMS, or self-modification.
key_findings.evidence: At 760M parameters/30B tokens, Hope reports WikiText perplexity 18.68, LAMBADA perplexity 20.07, and average commonsense accuracy 52.28 versus Titans 20.08/21.52/51.68. At 1.3B/100B, Hope reports 14.39/10.08/58.04 versus Titans 15.60/11.41/56.82 and Transformer 17.92/17.73/53.38. Learning rates are tuned per model and all are trained with AdamW; no matched total training/update FLOP or parameter decomposition for extra CMS levels is supplied.

anchors.section: Section 9.4 / Table 2 language modeling and commonsense reasoning

key_findings.claim: Hope has a clear short-context trade-off: the ordinary Transformer beats it on every reported recall-intensive task.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 gives Hope 65.9/21.2/22.8/41.9/33.0/57.7 across FDA, SWDE, SQUAD, NaturalQ, TriviaQA, and Drop, while Transformer gives 71.4/22.0/23.9/67.3/39.4/59.1. The authors explicitly attribute this to softmax attention's precise short-range retrieval, so Hope's long-context memory gains do not dominate dense attention universally.

key_findings.claim: On synthetic associative recall, Hope is best by a modest margin, while on formal languages it is not uniquely accurate.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 reports Hope 51.2/100/52.1/99.7/85.2 on the five MAD tasks versus Titans 49.8/100/50.0/99.4/83.4. Table 5 reports 100 on all 12 formal-language tasks for Hope, but LSTM and SRWM also score 100 on all 12; those alternatives are marked non-parallel whereas Hope is marked parallel. The novelty there is the accuracy/parallelism combination, not accuracy alone.

key_findings.claim: The ablation caption's claim that every component contributes positively is contradicted by its own language-modeling column.
key_findings.evidence: Table 6 gives full Hope perplexity 12.24 and reasoning 58.1. Removing the self-modifying query objective yields better perplexity 12.19, although reasoning falls to 57.4. Other removals worsen both reported metrics. Therefore every component contributes to the two-metric aggregate only under an unstated weighting; the query component does not positively contribute to perplexity in this run.

key_findings.claim: The continual-learning and extreme-context figures are promising proof-of-concept results but are not controlled demonstrations that catastrophic forgetting has been solved.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 6 compares Hope after 15B continual-pretraining tokens on class-incremental CLINC, Banking, and DBpedia and reports the highest bars, but provides no numeric labels, seeds, uncertainty, or matched parameter/update cost. Figures 8-9 show strong CTNL and BABILong curves, including approximately 94% at 10M for fine-tuned Hope, yet model/budget details are incomplete in the figure presentation. The conclusion explicitly says catastrophic forgetting is not solved.

key_findings.claim: The comparison protocol explicitly omits a strong direct competitor, Cartridges, from one long-context continual-learning figure because its memory and compute differ.
key_findings.evidence: The paper notes that Cartridges has shown promising and sometimes better performance, but excludes it because Hope uses a different memory/computational setup. That concern is legitimate, yet it also means the displayed figure is not a frontier comparison; the same matched-resource concern applies to Hope's extra memory levels relative to several included baselines.

key_findings.claim: M3 is slower than both Muon and AdaMuon in the reported runs, so 'on par with AdaMuon' is a qualitative interpretation rather than timing equivalence.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 12 plots approximately 43 versus 41 versus 38 hours for M3/AdaMuon/Muon on 140M and approximately 79 versus 75 versus 70 hours at 1.3B. Figure 11 suggests favorable ViT ImageNet-21K train/test curves for M3, but exact final values, seed variation, and a full matched-hyperparameter table are absent. M3 is presented as a proof-of-concept and adds a second momentum timescale plus matrix orthogonalization and variance normalization.

method.core_idea: Treat every adaptable component as an associative memory that compresses its own context under an internal objective; order components by update frequency to expose nested learning levels, then design deeper update rules and memory systems by adding levels, timescales, and self-referential parameter generators.
method.mechanism: The paper rewrites gradient-based optimizers as memory objectives, proposes DGD/delta momentum and the multi-timescale M3 optimizer, builds CMS from MLP memories updated at different chunk frequencies, and makes Titans self-modifying by turning its projections and update coefficients into in-context-updated memories. Hope composes self-modifying Titans with CMS, so a fast memory adapts within context while slower levels retain and transfer compressed knowledge.
assumptions: Any parameterized mapping trained under an internal objective may be called an associative memory, including layers, optimizers, and parameter generators.
Update frequency is a meaningful common coordinate for comparing pretraining, in-context updates, recurrent state, optimizer moments, and meta-learning loops.
Nested objectives and their context dependencies can be analyzed compositionally even when their simultaneous nonstationary dynamics are not solved.
The optimizer rewrites use local linearization, proximal objectives, constructed regression targets, and in the Adam case approximations to gradient statistics.
DGD assumes normalized inputs and uses an L2 mapping objective, although the printed derivation has inconsistent sign and reciprocal learning-rate conventions.
CMS can allocate redundant capacity at several chunk frequencies, and backpropagation can transfer recoverable knowledge between those levels.
Self-modifying Titans can stably update its key/value/query projections and update coefficients through nested MLP memories during a sequence.
Chunkwise forms approximate or implement the recurrent self-modification while retaining parallelizable training.
Comparisons with models at nominally similar parameter scales are informative despite unreported differences in active memory, update FLOPs, and tuned learning rates.
Long-context synthetic benchmarks and constructed continual-learning tasks are adequate proxies for persistent knowledge and general continual learning.

techniques.role: Represents learning components as interdependent optimization levels indexed by update frequency.
Rewrites GD, momentum, AdaGrad, and Adam using internal compression objectives.
Adds a state-dependent rank-one forgetting term to a gradient update through an L2 mapping objective.
Applies delta-rule retention to optimizer momentum for changing gradient contexts.
Stacks redundant MLP memory levels with different chunk/update frequencies.
Combines two momentum timescales with Newton-Schulz orthogonalization and Adam-like variance scaling.
Makes memory projections and update coefficients themselves in-context-updated associative memories.
Composes self-modifying Titans with CMS for long-context and continual-learning experiments.
Replaces the self-modifying recurrent memory with softmax attention to separate dense retrieval from CMS effects.
Groups recurrent memory updates into chunks to improve training parallelism.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3 3B/8B CMS variants with 15B continual-pretraining tokens on class-incremental CLINC, Banking, and DBpedia.
evaluations.metric: Average incremental task accuracy shown in Figure 6.
evaluations.result: Hope is the highest plotted method across the reported panels, but the figure gives no numeric labels, seeds, error bars, or matched update/parameter cost.
evaluations.baseline: ICL, EWC, InCA, and CMS/model variants.

evaluations.setting: NIAH benchmark at 4K-16K after roughly 50B training tokens.
evaluations.metric: Retrieval accuracy on three single-needle and multi-key, multi-query, and multi-value tasks.
evaluations.result: At 16K, Hope reports 78.2 on S-NIAH-2, 24.8 on S-NIAH-3, 14.8 MK, 14.2 MQ, and 11.4 MV; it is not best at every 4K single-needle cell.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer, RetNet, DeltaNet, DLA, Titans, Miras, and Hope-Attention.

evaluations.setting: BABILong after task fine-tuning, evaluated from ordinary context through 10M tokens.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy versus context length from Figure 9.
evaluations.result: Hope remains near 94% at 10M in the plotted curve, versus roughly 77% Titans, 69% ARMT, and 35% RAG; exact values and variance are not tabulated.
evaluations.baseline: Titans, ARMT, RAG, and large zero-shot long-context models.

evaluations.setting: 760M models trained on 30B tokens and 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens.
evaluations.metric: WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity plus average commonsense accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer, RetNet, DeltaNet, DLA, Titans, Samba, Miras, and other recurrent/hybrid models.

evaluations.setting: Six short-context recall-intensive datasets in Table 3.
MAD synthetic associative-recall suite and 12 formal-language tasks.
evaluations.result: Hope leads the five MAD columns at 51.2/100/52.1/99.7/85.2. Hope reaches 100 on all 12 formal languages, tied in accuracy with LSTM and SRWM while retaining the paper's parallel-training designation.
evaluations.baseline: Titans, DeltaNet, linear attention, LSTM, and SRWM.

evaluations.result: Full Hope is 12.24/58.1. Removing DGD, momentum, decay, CMS, inner key, or inner value worsens both; removing inner query yields 12.19/57.4, improving perplexity while lowering reasoning.
evaluations.baseline: Full Hope versus seven one-component removals.

evaluations.setting: ViT training on ImageNet-21K and language-model optimizer wall-clock at 140M and 1.3B.
evaluations.result: M3 has the favorable plotted ViT curve but takes about 43/79 hours versus AdaMuon 41/75 and Muon 38/70 at 140M/1.3B.
evaluations.baseline: AdamW, Muon, AdaMuon, and other optimizer variants.

limitations: Nested Learning's definitions are so inclusive that much of the conceptual contribution is a redescription; no falsifiable criterion separates systems that meaningfully benefit from NL from ordinary nested optimization.
The associative-memory interpretation depends on objectives and targets constructed to recover known updates, especially for Adam, and does not establish optimizer optimality for learning.
The DGD equations contain a material sign and reciprocal-step-size inconsistency, so the proposed printed update lacks a valid derivation as written.
No stability or convergence theorem is provided for DGD, CMS, self-modifying Titans, Hope, or M3.
Hope changes several factors simultaneously: recurrent memory, learned update mappings, decay, momentum, CMS depth, timescales, parameters, state, and compute.
Most comparisons are not matched for total parameters, active memory, training tokens, update FLOPs, or wall-clock; learning rates are tuned separately.
Several headline figures omit exact values, seeds, error bars, dataset sizes, and variance; no official implementation or reproducibility artifact is linked.

The continual-learning demonstrations use constructed class-incremental or new-language settings and large additional training budgets, and the conclusion acknowledges catastrophic forgetting remains unsolved.
Cartridges, an acknowledged strong long-context competitor, is omitted from one comparison because of resource differences, leaving the frontier comparison incomplete.
Softmax Transformer is clearly stronger on every reported short-context recall task, exposing a precision/retention trade-off.
Formal-language accuracy ties LSTM and SRWM, so the result does not establish unique computational capability.
The neuroscience motivation is analogical; no biological measurement validates the proposed frequency hierarchy or self-referential update mechanism.
failure_modes: DGD implemented from equation (113) will differ in sign and step-size scaling from DGD implemented from equations (114)-(121).
Coupled self-modifying memories can generate unstable learning rates, projections, or forgetting coefficients during an unseen sequence.
Fast CMS levels can overwrite recent information before slow levels absorb it; slow levels can preserve stale or conflicting knowledge.
Increasing CMS levels can appear to improve retention simply by adding redundant parameters, memory state, and compute.
Chunkwise updates can lose token-level order or introduce boundary artifacts relative to the recurrent definition.
Attention-free compression can lose exact short-range details, consistent with Hope's losses to Transformer on all six short recall tasks.
Self-generated key/value/query mappings can collapse, become mutually inconsistent, or amplify noisy contexts without an external correctness signal.
A method tuned on synthetic NIAH/BABILong retrieval can fail on semantic long-document reasoning or continually changing real data.
Per-model learning-rate tuning and unequal compute can turn an architecture comparison into a hyperparameter/budget comparison.
Continual pretraining can improve new-task bars while silently degrading unmeasured prior capabilities.
Nested terminology can obscure rather than resolve which objective, state, timescale, or gradient path causally produces a gain.
The M3 second momentum path adds wall-clock cost and can be redundant or harmful when landscape frequencies do not separate cleanly.
reusable_insights: Indexing memory components by update frequency is a useful design and audit language, provided parameter, state, and compute costs are reported per level.
Optimizer updates can be studied as online regression/memory rules, but derived objectives should be distinguished from explanatory or optimality theorems.
Multi-timescale memory should be evaluated with controlled equal-capacity and equal-compute ablations, not only by adding levels.
A self-modifying model needs explicit stability constraints and diagnostics for generated learning rates, retention gates, and projection drift.
Report both exact short-range retrieval and long-range retention because compressed recurrent memories and softmax attention have complementary failure profiles.
For continual learning, measure retained old-task capability, new-task acquisition, compute, memory growth, and forward/backward transfer together.
Audit every algebraic optimizer proposal by differentiating its printed objective and checking signs, units, and reciprocal learning-rate conventions.
Keep representational unification, architectural novelty, and empirical superiority as separate claims with separate evidence.
open_questions: What corrected objective and parameter convention did the authors intend for DGD, and do corrected variants reproduce Hope's ablation gains?
Can CMS or Hope be shown stable and non-forgetting under a defined stream model with bounded capacity?
Do Hope's gains persist under exactly matched parameters, optimizer state, update FLOPs, tokens, and wall-clock?
Which of self-modification, DGD, momentum, retention, and CMS timescales causally accounts for each benchmark gain?
How do generated update rules behave under adversarial, contradictory, or distribution-shifted contexts?
Can a common benchmark compare Hope, Cartridges, Titans, ATLAS, TTT, and softmax attention at matched serving and training costs?
Does the NL vocabulary yield new testable predictions that cannot be derived from standard bilevel optimization, meta-learning, fast weights, or dynamical-systems analyses?
Can the short-context recall deficit be removed without giving up subquadratic long-context behavior?

competitive_landscape.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct architectural predecessor and principal baseline: neural long-term memory updated at test time.
competitive_landscape.difference: Titans updates a memory under a fixed learned rule and has no CMS; Nested Learning makes the projections/update rule self-modifying and adds multiple frequency levels in Hope.

competitive_landscape.title: It's All Connected: A Journey Through Test-Time Memorization, Attentional Bias, Retention, and Online Optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: MIRAS is the closest conceptual predecessor, unifying sequence models as associative memories with choices of objective, retention, and online optimizer.
competitive_landscape.difference: Nested Learning expands the taxonomy to nested optimization frequencies, optimizer memories, self-generated update modules, CMS, and M3; much of its associative-memory vocabulary is inherited rather than new.

competitive_landscape.title: ATLAS: Learning to Optimally Memorize the Context at Test Time
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct same-author competitor for higher-capacity and non-online test-time memory, including long-context BABILong gains.
competitive_landscape.difference: ATLAS improves the memory objective/capacity and past-token optimization; Hope instead emphasizes a self-modifying rule plus a hierarchy of update frequencies.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational modern test-time-training architecture whose recurrent hidden state is itself a learned model updated by a self-supervised objective.
competitive_landscape.difference: TTT uses a fixed test-time learning rule for TTT-Linear/MLP; Nested Learning adds self-referential rule adaptation, optimizer nesting, and multiple memory timescales.

competitive_landscape.title: Cartridges: Lightweight and General-Purpose Long Context Representations via Self-Study
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strong direct alternative for persistent, amortizable long-context memory and continual knowledge incorporation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cartridges trains a compact corpus-specific KV representation offline with synthetic self-study and reports serving memory/throughput; Hope updates recurrent nested memories and targets online continual adaptation. The target paper acknowledges but omits Cartridges from one figure.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary predecessor equating linear attention with fast-weight associative memory and introducing delta-rule corrections and learned learning rates.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already supplies the memory-programming and delta-update foundation; Nested Learning generalizes the vocabulary to optimizers/nested levels and uses deep self-modifying memories plus CMS.

competitive_landscape.title: A Modern Self-Referential Weight Matrix That Learns to Modify Itself
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior primary architecture for a scalable weight matrix that modifies itself during runtime.
competitive_landscape.difference: SRWM uses self-referential outer-product/delta programming and demonstrates few-shot/RL performance; Hope extends self-reference to deep projection/update memories and combines it with a multi-frequency CMS.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Continual Learning Assisted by an External Continual Learner
competitive_landscape.relationship: Official continual-learning baseline used by the target, combining frozen-LLM ICL with a compact external class selector.
competitive_landscape.difference: InCA avoids updating the LLM and scales prompts by class preselection; Hope continually changes internal memories and targets a broader sequence-model architecture, with different compute and forgetting risks.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present Nested Learning as a new paradigm that unifies architectures and optimizers as nested associative memories, introduces expressive optimizers, a self-modifying learning module, Continuum Memory Systems, and the Hope architecture with broad empirical gains.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives formal context-flow/nesting definitions, constructed optimizer objectives, DGD/delta momentum/M3 updates, three CMS arrangements, a deep self-referential Titans formulation, and Hope/Hope-Attention experiments across continual learning, NIAH, BABILong, language modeling, recall, MAD, formal languages, and vision optimization.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The most distinctive contribution is the synthesis of self-modifying test-time memory with an explicit hierarchy of update frequencies and its broad Hope prototype. The umbrella claim is less novel than the artifact: fast weights, delta rules, self-referential matrices, TTT, Titans, MIRAS, and ATLAS already cover much of the conceptual territory. Evidence is proof-of-concept rather than a demonstrated new paradigm, and the core DGD algebra is inconsistent as printed. Claims of universal empirical superiority should be narrowed because Transformer wins every short-recall task, Titans wins some NIAH cells, LSTM/SRWM tie formal-language accuracy, one ablation improves perplexity, Cartridges is omitted, and costs/variance are incompletely controlled.
